speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before this bill is read the second time, will the government say that it is the only legislation of the kind that they have in mind, and if they intend' to christen it with the title, Rural Credits?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for agricultural credits largely along the lines of the recommendations of Dr. Tory who made a report upon the subject to the Banking and Commerce committee. The fundamental principle of the bill is co-operatior. between the Dominion and the provinces. The bill provides that no advance shall be made to any province unless the province agrees that such advance shall constitute a debt of the province to the Dominion, secured by bonds of the province to an. amount equal to the advance. There is also a provision that as a condition of the advance the province shall provide by law a summary means of collecting both interest and principal satisfactory to the Governor in Council, and that no charge, lien, or other encumbrance representing any tax or other claim shall rank ahead of the first mortgage. This will probably require in some provinces a change in the provincial law.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The minister has carefully dodged the question. May I put it this way: It is really only a joke to call this legislation Rural Credits. It is a loan to the provinces. Has any province asked for this?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: There have been representations made to us in this House by the representatives of different provinces.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Have the representatives of any of the provincial governments asked for this legislation?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I am coming to that in a moment. I am bound to admit that there is some division of opinion on the matter among the different provinces. Some already have a rural credit scheme, while others have a farm loan scheme; some have proved profitable, others not so. We advance this as a measure satisfactory to those hon. gentlemen who have been urging it upon us, and it will be for each province to determine whether or not it will enter into the scheme.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Have any of the provinces asked for this legislation? The question has not yet been answered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, possibly I may be able to enlighten mv hon. friends to the right. The province

of Alberta has passed legislation respecting long term rural credits, but the minister in charge, Hon. Mr. Brownlee, made it quite clear before the measurp passed the local house that to make it operative it would be necessary that they should be able to raise money by cheaper means such as through the Dominion government, than they are now able to do as a province. subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I am willing to concede the government credit for savi lg itself in this matter, but frankly I do not look upon the measure as by any means ample enough to meet the requirements of an agricultural loan scheme for the Dominion. I am, however, not at this moment objecting to the little bit that is offered, especially as I hope that further reasons in the future will induce the government to realize that a ten-million-dollar loan will not in any way effe.t what is the chief purpose of the bill-the reduction of the interest rates on long tern mortgages. In Saskatchewan, under the run! credit system something over nine million dollars has already been loaned without materially, or indeed appreciably, producing any effect upon t'he level of interest rates on long term loans in that province. Dr. Tory, in cross-examination before the committee on Agriculture of 1924, made it quite clear that in his opinion it would require from sixteen to twenty per cent of the total amount of money now outstanding in farm loans to be loaned in competition under some government scheme to be effective in reducing interest rates.

Any municipality desiring to borrow money for the purpose of lending the same to farmers in such municipality may do so upon passing a resolution at any regular meeting of the municipal council of Buch municipality, or at a special meeting duly called for that purpose, setting forth that the municipality wishes to borrow a sum of money, not exceeding a specific amount, repayable annually at the rate of five per cent per annum.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I know what is in my hon. friend's mind, I think. His point is that the provincial bonds are selling almost on a par with federal bonds, and that therefore in the issue of farm loan bonds there is no advantage in having the federal government as guarantor. That, of course, is very largely a matter of opinion. My own opinion is that there will be advantage in having the backing of the federal government in the issue of these bonds covering farm loans.
But what I wanted particularly to say is this. I am more attracted to the scheme suggested and discussed and written about at some length 'by Mr. Petersen of Calgary. His scheme would provide for a system of rural credits that would be financed largely by the people themselves. Still, I know the difficulty in the inception of a scheme of that kind.
I do believe, however, that if the rural sections of Canada are to be successful in securing cheap money, it will have to be done in some manner other than continually leaning upon the credit of the provinces or of the federal government. We have a serious situation in Canada, particularly in western Canada, where the interest rates are much higher than in any other part of this country, where money is dearer, and transportation and living costs are higher, and relief in this direction I think should be extended to these provinces. I do

Rural Credits
not think it should be extended to them to an extent beyond what their credit will warrant. Under this bill the government are not taking any chance of having losses, but this step is being taken for the time being in order to inaugurate a system of this kind. We are loaning our credit to the extent of $10,000,000. It is true that $10,000,000 will not go very far in a scheme of this kind, but I think it will go far enough to meet the requirements at least of this year. It will take some considerable time to get the negotiations worked out between the provinces who are desirous of obtaining loans and the federal government. No one would argue that $10000,000 would be of any advantage at all if it were to be confined to that. I think Doctor Tory is well within the mark when he states that the farm loan indebtedness of the three prairie provinces is well over $200,000,000. Some years ago when I was premier of the province of Alberta-at the time, by the way, when our farm loan bill was passed-the indebtedness of the province of Alberta alone was then $60,000,000, so that to suggest that $10,000,000 would meet the situation is an utter absurdity. But I would like in the intervening period between this session and next to make some further study of the scheme. I see no difficulty in encouraging under provincial auspices, backed by the credit of the federal government farm loan societies much along the same lines as our rural credit societies are being carried on to-day. That is what I would like to see done, but I do think it is important that the credit of the federal government be behind the scheme in order to get the money at the cheapest rate.

speechtext: If the minister has not that in his own head he has not given much study to this subject. Rural credits in Manitoba are based on the idea of government cooperative units. subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:

measure should have been entitled " An Act to relieve the Loan Companies of Bad Loans."

Hon. gentlemen to my left should not take this too seriously, or be too technical in their objections to the different clauses. It will only be a waste of time. lending a dollar to any province under the bill. There are clauses in the bill which give him the absolute control, and he can sit tight and do as he likes, which will make the province hang right back and not even apply.

speechtext: This measure says that the loan which the province makes is going to rank ahead of taxes and liens of any kind. How many municipalities are going to stftnd for that? However, we might as well pass the bill and get through with it. The result will be the same as if the bill were defeated. We can pass it and in that way defeat it. Hon. gentlemen probably desire to get home. This is so much propaganda, to cover the event of a possible election, so that the government will be able to say that they met the demands of the hon. gentleman from Bow River (Mr. Garland) for a rural credit scheme. speechtext: The right hon. leader of the opposition is very sarcastic this morning in regard to this bill.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Wait and see.
[Mr. Forke.J

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I think he is wrong in regard to the Farm Loan Association in Manitoba. I am fairly well acquainted with the work of that institution, and I think its loans have been made with just as much care as the mortgage companies loans have been made, and perhaps the association is in better condition as far as the farm loans are concerned than the majority of the mortgage corporations in Manitoba.
The rural credit scheme is on a different footing. I have no fault to find with the Rural Credit Act in Manitoba, but I have fault to find with the way it has been worked out. I do not care what laws or what acts you have, there is always a human element-that enters into it. and that is where the Manitoba rural credit scheme has fallen down. The local board has been t-oo sympathetic and too ready to make loans. There is another situation that has rather worked against the successful carrying out of the act. The act came into force at the time when prices were very high, and loans were largely made upon the valuation put upon the property by those seeking the loans. While the loan was perfectly safe at that time, according to the valuation that had been made, in a year or two, when values had shrunk very rapidly the loans were not so well secured and no doubt there has been a loss. The weakness of the whole situation has been that the local board has not been selected with sufficient care. I do not think it is wrong for me to say here that in some cases local merchants and others who were interested in collecting the debts from those who were borrowing money were on that board, and a favourite arrangement was to advise the borrower to consolidate his debt. That is to borrow sufficient money to pay off bis local debt, and then apply to the rural credit society. Hon. gentlemen can see how it worked out. He paid the debt, but left a large debt to the rural credit society, and they made failures, while the merchants got their money.
I have something to say about the trouble in borrowing money. The trouble in the west is that the security is not always good. You cannot expect to borrow money unless you are able to put up security.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I think that is correct.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Everywhere.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
And that is really the crux of the whole situation. The serious state of the agricultural industry, and the difficulty in making agriculture a paying proposition

Rural Credits
brings up a serious difficulty in borrowing money for agricultural purposes. Loan societies, governments, or any other institutions like to see how their loan is going to be repaid. We find the west has got into difficulties. Farmers have got into difficulties and municipalities, provincial governments and other institutions, have tried to ease the load of the farmer as far as possible. We find the provincial government passing laws one after the other to prevent foreclosure, to make sure that those 'who have loaned money in any way can get it back at some future time. Consequently when you have that state of affairs interest immediately rises, and a difficulty in securing loans occurs. I do not think that we are ever going to have any successful borrowing or loaning institutions until we get things put on a more profitable footing.
Then the difficulty arises with regard to the occupation of agriculture. How are we going to put agriculture on a safe basis, unless we have funds? I hoped the government would have some scheme to bring before the House in order to show us some way out of the difficulty. There is nothing in the scheme that I can see to help us out, for the simple reason that if the security is good the provinces can borrow the money themselves, and if they have to become good for the money they might just as well borrow in the first place. I do not see that there is anything in this bill. I do not like to condemn it. It may be an honest attempt to relieve the situation. Ten million dollars may be only a beginning. The only point in my opinion is that if the Dominion government can borrow much cheaper than the provinces, it might be an advantage for them to borrow the money and loan it to the provinces. That is the only advantage that I can see in a scheme of this kind, but I do not know that they can borrow it so much more advantageously than the provinces. I agree with the criticism that has been made of the amount-ten million dollars.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: What scheme of rural credit would my hon. friend advocate?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am not advocating any.
I know that it is very popular in some quarters. The only plan that I think would be feasible is the amortization plan of long term loans at low interest; but you must get security to carry out that plan, and that is why we emphasize so much in this part of the House the tremendous necessity of putting agriculture on a prosperous basis. The whole question arises simply because there is so
much difficulty about security. I seriously think the ten-million^dollar proposition is just a joke; it would not begin to do anything, so far as rural credits are concerned.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Referring to the system
adopted in the United States, of long term credits, can my hon. friend tell me how much the United States advanced to the federal
farm loan boards?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I think that is a different scheme altogether and is not in the same position as this at all.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Why not advocate the same plan in Canada?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
That is a different thing.
The only proposition that I would advocate in the way of Dominion government loaning would be to loan, not ten million, but probably a hundred million-I would not like to mention the exact sum-and to loan that money under the amortization plan, namely loqg term loans at low interest. Perhaps it could be loaned at five per cent for twenty or thirty years on fairly good security. In that way I think something could be done to help the west. No ten-million-dollar scheme is ever going to accomplish anything at all. The Minister of the Interior says that this is a trial. Well it is a failure to begin with, if we only start with ten millions.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I have never spoken in the House before, and I only do so now because I have always looked upon the farmer as the Atlas, from an economic viewpoint, of the industry of the whole world. Holding that view, I think I should for a short time deal with the proposition before the House. Several hon. gentlemen have spoken slightingly of the amount proposed in the bill

S10,-000,000. If they would give some consideration to the long term credit system of the United States, they would think $10,000,000 would be ample to sustain the long term credit of the Dominion of Canada. I have before me the report of last year, that is Dr. Tory's first report, and I find that twelve federal land banks were established in the United States, these banks coinciding in position with the twelve federal reserve banks. I find the capitalization, money advanced by the federal government of the United States for each of these banks, was $750,000, making for the twelve banks a total of $9,000,000. That would appear to be a small sum to finance a mortgage scheme on the amortization plan for the whole of the United States, a country with about 115,000,000 people. But that grant has been ample. I 'hold in my
Rural Credits

hand t/he last report from the Secretary of the Treasury, and I find in it that the net mortgage loans to-day amount to $927,000,000 odd. The liabilities of the institution are farm land bonds outstanding, $914,000,000 odd. And the only capital held by the United States in these banks is $1,670,000. At no time have the United States been asked to advance more than their initial loan of $9,000,000. How has that been done? It has been done by a revolving scheme. I can illustrate that in a very few words. When a man gives a mortgage for $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 on his farm, that mortgage is turned into what is called a mortgage bond. Those mortgage bonds are sold' and, according to a letter I hold in my hand, those mortgage bonds in the United States are picked up like hot cakes. They have met with a ready sale from the very inception of .the scheme; so much so that many of those who hold mortgage bonds in the United States to-day can sell them at a premium.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Why do those mortgage bonds sell at a premium.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Because the security is good.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Is it not also because they are tax free?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am aware of all those facts. I am well aware of the fact that the $9,000,000 advanced by the United States was advanced to the farmers free of interest. I am well aware of the fact that the bonds sold are free from federal, state and municipal taxation, indeed all taxation of any description whatever. Further, I know the Unites States government makes no demands in connection with the dividends accruing through this system. They have placed the farmers there on a very good basis. The money that was advanced to them cost the farmers not one cent of interest to the United States government, notwithstanding the fact that it cost the United States government between 3i and 4 per cent to raise the money. Why should any hon. member in any comer of this House object to that? That was something given to the farmers of the United States; were they not deserving of it? Could the man who is doing business under the sheltering aegis of a tariff of thirty-five or forty per cent complain? Certainly not. I advocate here today and I believe this $10,000,000 will be all that this government will be asked to advance. I would ask for the advance of that money without charging the farmers of this country one cent of interest. I would also advocate the American system of tax exemp-
tion on all bonds connected with a system of this kind. How can this be done? Every province, by this initial move, can stand on its own- feet as an individual unit. Why cannot the provinces institute a bureau in connection with their individual treasury departments? Why cannot they take these long term mortgages for twenty, thirty, forty or forty-five years, turn them into mortgage-bonds and sell them? Why cannot a scheme similar to the revolving system in the United States finance itself? I feel safe in saying that an average advance of $1,000,000 to each of the provinces will be amply sufficient to finance this whole scheme and bring relief to the farmers of the Dominion.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Is the hon. memfoer advocating the establishment of a rural credit system or a long term farm loan system similar to that in the United States?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am confining my remarks
-and I thought I was quite clear-to what we call long term credits on the amortization principle. While on that point I should like to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that what we call the short term credits and intermediate credits, which are in existence in the United States to-day, have been in existence for only a little over one year- not two years yet. I have evidence in a work which I hold in my hand that the system so far, as the writer says, has not . proved an unqualified success. Hence I would not at the present time advocate a system of short term credits or intermediate credits as that system in the United States is now only on trial, having been instituted less than two years ago. I have a letter from a gentleman known to almost every member in this House, Mr. Tom King, and th:s is what he says:
Now, as I wrote you, the mortgages held by the federal farm loan boards only amount to $1,300,000,000.
That was the amount of mortgages held by the federal farm loan board in the United States. The farm mortgages in the United States amount to from $13,000,000,000 to $18,000,000,000, so that only a small part of the indebtedness is carried by the farm loan boards at the present time. As a matter oi fact, I believe it is only about seven per cent. Let me read from this communication from Mr. King. He says:
From the standpoint of the farmer, of course, it has been a great success. But you will be told in Canada that the United States treasury has been-depleted to lend all this money. Now, as a matter of fact, out of the nine million dollars voted less than. $2,000,000 was furnished bv the United States government.

Rural Credits
488?
I call attention to that fact:
When the banks were organized, the government *subscribed for stock to the amount of $9,000,000.
I would emphasize this point. All the stock has been retired with the exception of $1,870,000. At the inception of the organization the farmers were loaned $9,000,000; that was the limit. And of this amount the United States government advanced not more than $2,000,000. The farmers have paid back the whole amount advanced them, and they owe only $1,670,000 to the government. So that it is only a matter of two or three years until the system is self-sustaining, passing out of the hands of the government altogether into the control of the farmers. The scheme was so managed that the farmers were put in a position to finance it themselves within a short time, and will control it from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Does the hon. member contend that this legislation now before parliament will inaugurate such a scheme as exists in the United States?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I am not pretending that for a moment, although as a matter of fact I think that you are getting something better. I believe that the $10,000,000 provided for in this bill is quite sufficient. There should be no necessity to call upon the government to advance one more dollar if each of the provinces adopting the scheme would establish a bureau in connection with the provincial finance department to manage the thing, as they will have power to do. No large organization will be necessary, and there is no reason why the scheme should not be successful if run on the same lines exactly as the one under the federal farm loan board of the United States. To me it is a simple matter. By converting the mortgages into mortgage bonds and selling the bonds the scheme can be made selfsustaining and more than self-sustaining.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that by this very legislation the money to be provided here is forbidden to be used in the way the United States board uses its funds?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I do know that the long
term credit scheme in the United States has so far proved an absolute success. There may have been a few foreclosures, but this is bound to happen anywhere, and the generai result has been so satisfactory that the organization has lost nothing.
We have in Ontario both a long term and a short term system and in connection with the long term loans there has not been the loss of one dollar on the part of the provincial government. I would however advocate a system somewhat different. The land is valued in Ontario by one valuator and improper valuations are apt to be made in some cases; but in the United States three members of the local board appraise the land, and in addition there is a federal appraiser who visits the various units and makes an independent valuation. The long term system in Ontario has been an undoubted success, and I see no reason *why this scheme should not be equally satisfactory, especially if we adopted some system such as they have in the United States. It would take some time to organize it properly but we have the United States model to copy from. And they have the best rural credit system in the world.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member call the United States rural credit system a national or a state system?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: It is of course a national scheme, but I am convinced that the plan proposed in this legislation will be successful. So far as I am aware, there is no demand on the part of the Ontario government for any help or direction from this parliament, nor is there such a demand from the province of Quebec. Indeed, I do not think that there is any practical demand from any province of the Dominion for federal control. Some of the provinces may be so wedded to their own schemes that they would not care to adopt a federal system, and I do not think that the Dominion government would be acting wisely if it superimposed any national scheme upon the local units. I am sure that if we adopted in each of the provinces some system corresponding to the federal system cf the United States, the small sum of $10,000,000 would be ample to finance the individual undertakings in such a way that the active units would be able to pay back the money to the Dominion in a few years, become self-sustaining, and pass entirely into the control of the farmers themselves.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I want to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on bringing down this bill, but I must express regret that he has seen fit to introduce, forty-eight hours before prorogation, a measure of such importance. A better act than this has been asked for during the past three years by members of western Canada and it is not in the interests of the country that legislation of this importance should be brought down in the last hours of the session and possibly of this parliament. Rural credit legislation is asked for by the people of the west particularly, for the simple reason that

Rural Credits
the present banking facilities are not in the best interests of agriculture. The time limit on notes is too short, the interest rates are too high, and the renewals are too uncertain. With regard to chattel mortgages, also, the time is too short, the interest rates and expenses are too high. It is for these reasons that for some years past there has been an agitation for a system of rural credits. We have continually asked this parliament for a measure of relief. We all know that agriculture has been going through a very strenuous time during the past several years. We have asked for bread; in this bill we have been given a stone. As the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) says, it is doubtful whether a single dollar will be asked for under this legislation, surrounded as it is with so many restrictions.
The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) wanted to know if the provinces had made any demand for such legislation, and the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. McKay) asked the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) if he had any scheme to suggest. Now, I am going to place before the House a very carefully thought-out scheme that has been put forward by the Alberta Provincial U.F.A. Convention, -which has been asking for rural credit legislation, but before doing so I want to refer to the suggestion made by the hon. member for North Renfrew that for a rural credit scheme we should issue tax-free bonds, x do net agree with him. I think tax-free bonds are absolutely wrong. It simply means that men with surplus wealth would invest in those bonds, their investment would not be taxable, and the extra taxation would have to be paid by the masses of the people who cannot so well afford to shoulder the burden. The scheme to which I referred was put forward by the United Farmers of Alberta at their annual convention, extending from January 20 to January 23, 1925, and is contained in the following resolution, which was adopted unanimously:
Whereas the question of rural credits and the relief of agriculture by providing cheaper money for farmers, has become within the past ten years one of the chief economic problems of this continent, and in this country has now reached a condition so acute as to become a national crisis; and
Whereas, efficient methods of meeting this situation can only be inaugurated by action by the Dominion parliament; and
Whereas the Finance Act, 1923, provides that advances of Dominion notes may be made to the chartered banks by the Treasury Board on the deposit of approved securities, among which as listed and actually received by the board, provincial bonds are deemed to be of the first rank as security, such securities held by the Treasury Board taking the place of any gold

redemption reserve in so far as such issues of Dominion notes are concerned, and
Whereas, such provincial bonds when deposited with the Treasury Board by the province are of exactly the same value as securities as when deposited by a bank;
Be it therefore resolved that this convention urge upon our federal representatives to use every effort to have action taken at the coming session of parliament to inaugurate a system of rural credits embracing the following principles:-
(a)	That the provinces be given the right to obtain from the Treasury Board, on the deposit of provincial bonds as security therefor, advances of Dominion notes for the purpose of rural credits.
(b)	Such right of a province to obtain such funds to take effect only on the passing of a resolution by the provincial legislature in favour of such action.
(c)	That interest on such advances be paid by the province to the Dominion at such rate as may be agreed upon, having in view the cost of establishment and operation of the system, such payments to be applied on the reduction of our national debt.
(d)	Such funds so obtained to be loaned to actual farmers on first mortgage security under strict .government supervision and appraisal up to fifty per cent of the appraised value of the land, such appraisals to b - based on the productive value of the land.
(e)	Such funds to be loaned at a rate of interest not exceeding one per cent greater than the rate paid by the province.
(f)	Loans to be made on a long term amortization plan of such length that the combined payment on principal and interest shall in no case exceed an additional payment of one per cent of the total indebtedness.
The United Farmers of Alberta have for several years past gone on record as advocating that a provincial bank should be established to relieve agriculture in the province. But it was recognized from what took place before the Banking and Commerce committee in 1923 that even if a charter was asked for to establish such a bank there would be very little chance of getting the measure through this parliament, and that was one of the reasons why at their last convention they decided to ask for relief through some other channel. Hence the resolution which I have placed before the House.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Is that a provincial or a local body?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Provincial. It was the intention to send a copy of the resolution to the Acting Minister of Finance, but it was thought that as the matter would probably come up before the Banking and Commerce committee it would be preferable to have the federal members from Alberta bring the scheme before the committee for discussion there. Unfortunately, we did not have that opportunity. I sincerely hope the Acting Minister of Finance will give the resolution his careful attention.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the minister upon the great courage he has had in bringing this legislation before the House and calling it a national farm loans scheme. As far as I am concerned, this legislation does not begin to touch the question at. all, and I do not think the minister realizes the tremendous problem that we have in western Canada to secure money for farmers at reasonable rates of interest. True, this measure may be a beginning towards that desirable end, but, not having any idea as to what is the ultimate intention of the minister, it is hard for me to accept his proposal as being even a beginning in the direction of long term farm loans.
Under our banking system, to all intents and purposes we turn over the total credit of Canada for the use of the banks, and in that connection we have what is known as the Finance Act of 1914. Under that act, which came into force because of war conditions, the chartered banks were empowered to obtain in advance of Dominion notes on depositing certain approved securities with the Treasury board. In the first place, these dominion notes are issued against the total credit of Canada, and all the producers in Canada are responsible for the creation of that credit. The basis of real credits in this or any other country is the ability to produce and deliver goods and services, and just to the extent that Canada can produce and deliver goods and services, to that extent only has Canada a real credit. Take agriculture, for instance; we probably produce very nearly half the real credit for Canada, yet when we want to put a portion of that credit into circulation we must go to a bank or some other financial institution, we must do that before we can use the real credit that we have produced. Under these circumstances it is impossible for agriculturists in Canada to get money at a reasonable rate of interest. In view of the fact that the banks have the privilege of taking provincial bonds to the Treasury board and securing an issue of Dominion notes against that provincial security, why should it not be just as feasible to allow the provincial government to place their bonds with the Treasury board and
receive a similar issue of Dominion notes for the purpose of making long term farm loans? Is there any reason why the provincial government should not do that? By that means the man who produces the real credit, the farmer himself, would be in a position to put a portion of his credit into circulation, and he could put it into circulation at cost. We have a financial system here in Canada that is laying a heavy hand upon the producers, and I am satisfied that before very long we will have to take drastic steps to get away from the heavy load we are carrying. I am willing to accept this legislation as far as it goes, but unless it is followed by something more effective it will not begin to cure the disease we are suffering from at the present time. This country is spending annually something like $3,500,000 to bring in immigrants, and what position are they in when they come here? If they have a little capital and desire to take up farming, they immediately become indebted to these loan companies for advances of money at high rates of interest. I am satisfied that no immigration scheme, unless it is linked up with a reasonable measure of rural credits in order to give these people a start, can be the success that we would like it to be. While this legislation is a beginning, I hope the minister will take the matter into consideration to a greater extent than he has done in the past and see if he cannot evolve some national rural credit scheme that will give the farmers the money at a reasonable rate of interest.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE-LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
In venturing a few remarks on this bill I hope the minister will not regard my comments as being of a destructive nature. I propose to deal with it from what I consider a constructive standpoint. The necessity for some form of rural credits is universally recognized in Canada. In his report Dr. Tory said:
It must be obvious to any one who gives this question serious consideration that some immediate improvement in methods of agricultural finance is imperative if Canada is to maintain her place in world agriculture. .
I notice a great deal of propaganda in the press lately condemning the principle of rural credits. It is pointed out by representatives of the mortgage companies that there is no necessity for a rural credit system because there is plenty of money on the market today. I do not think that is denied; I think we all recognize that there is sufficient money in Canada. But that is not the problem that the farmer has to face; the point is that he has to pay eight to ten per cent for the money, and that is the great problem that he
Rural Credits

has to grapple with. I notice that the Dominion Mortgage and Investment Association, whose head office is in Toronto, presented a memorandum to the government some time ago setting forth certain reasons why in their opinion the government should not undertake anything in the way of rural credits. This association of mortgage companies has been more concerned, I think, in maintaining high rates of interest than in trying to assist the country generally. It is commonly said-and I notice it is set forth in this memorandum presented to the government-that the farmers to-day are suffering from too much credit rather than not enough. I do not know that that is denied. There was a period during the war and immediately succeeding the war when there was too much credit in the country, and that applied to manufacturers, to business men and to railway corporations as well as to farmers. Then there was a period when our currency 'was inflated to such an extent that there was a surplus of money in the hands of these corporations, and they had to get it out. They got it out in the best way they could, and succeeded in getting the whole community into debt. What we are trying to deal with to-day is not to secure more money for the farmers. I want to make it clear that the farmer is not asking for more money, and I do not understand that it is the policy of the government to lend more money to them. The idea is to give the farmer an opportunity to borrow the necessary money to pay off his present indebtedness and spreading it over a long period of years at a greatly reduced 'rate of interest. I appreciate, of course, the fact that the government have done something, and I appreciate it more because it is a recognition of the necessity for rural credits measure than for what is actually contained in the bill before us. I hope it is the beginning of a larger plan that will eventually solve the problem so far as our farmers are concerned. Dr. Tory, in his report presented to parliament in 1924, dealt particularly with land bank system of the United States, and I think he made it clear to anyone who has intelligently studied that report that the problem has been dealt with very efficiently in the United States. He points out that the mortgage companies in Canada to-day are operating under a tremendous expense. They are suffering from what the Iron, member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has repeatedly pointed out in this House that the railways are suffering from-to much duplication. You will find five, six, seven or eight, sometimes nine or ten mortgage companies operating around one small village in western Canada, 
with seven or eight different appraisers going into that district every year to collect, to appraise the land and generally to oversee their business. That, to my mind, is the fundamental problem. Now, by pooling all these organizations their expenses could be cut down to a very great extent, and that is the principle on which the land bank system of the United States is based, namely, to cut out duplication by consolidating all these organizations and thus to reduce the cost of interest to the farmer. Now, in dealing with the land bank system of the United States. Dr. Tory said:
I think it cannot be denied, referring especially to Western Canada, that the mortgage business is conducted in an exceedingly expensive manner, and that reasonable co-op ration between land companies might greatly reduce the present cost of administration. The federal land banks of the United States are to-day conducting their business on a margin of one per cent and are setting aside out of that a considerable margin for possible losses.
He points out further that every country in the civilized world has ultimately been compelled to take such steps as this. He points out also that the federal land banks have conducted the business at a cost of one per cent and have paid back, in addition to interest on the capital stock which is held by farmers, almost the entire loan advanced to the land banks by the federal government. Now, my complaint with regard to the policy adopted by the minister is this: that the farmer is put in the humiliating position of borrowing money direct from the government treasury. I do not think that is a sound principle. I do not think the farmer should be loaned money direct by any government. What they are asking for and what Doctor Tory particularly recommended is that legislation be put through this House that would enable the farmer to stand fairly and squarely on his own feet, that would enable him to pool his own credit. The question may be asked, why cannot the farmer do that to-day, why cannot he do it without coming to this House for legislation? He cannot do it for the simple reason that the government has been responsible for a bank act which gives a monopoly of the handling of money to certain corporations, and before we can build up this land bank system it is necessary to have some legislation that will enable the farmers to do what the farmers of the United States have done in recent years, and what the farmers of Germany did over a century ago. This land bank system would 'be built up entirely by the farmers themselves. Each farmer asking for a loan would be compelled to leave five per cent of that loan in the

Rural Credits
treasury of the bank. Now that becomes capital stock. The farmer would be given a stock certificate for the amount, and when loans are asked for, a bond issue would be floated at the most convenient point in the country, the point where money was the most plentiful, and the loan would be issued, not against one farm mortgage-there would be no loan to one farmer by a man purchasing a bond direct-but the loan would be against the pooled credit of thousands of farmers.
Now the difference between such a system and the way the present mortgage companies do business is this. The mortgage companies loan to one single farmer. That farmer may be a poor farmer, he may fail completely, he may allow his taxes and interest to run into arrears until finally, when he is closed out, the mortgage company suffers a heavy loss. On the other hand, he may be a good farmer; it may be that he has done everything that he could possibly do, but that his particular district has suffered from hail, or frost, or rust, or some of the other thousand and one ills that agriculture is heir to. Under the particular system I suggest the purchaser of a bond in Montreal or New York would have as his security, not the earning power of one particular farmer, but the joint earning power of thousands of farmers, and if one of these mortgages had to be foreclosed, the loss spread over thousands of cases would be so small that it would be infinitesimal so far as the bondholder is concerned.
In addition to that, each farmer would have five per cent of his loan as stock in the bank. That is additional security, because the assets of the bank stand behind these bonds. That looks to me as a perfectly sound principle, a principle under which the farmer is enabled to stand fairly and squarely on his own feet, dnd not to have to lean on either the provincial or the federal treasury. The government would simply provide the necessary legislation to enable him to do that, and instead of having half a dozen or a dozen loan agents travelling around one little district in western Canada as they are doing to-day-I have seen as many as three at one time at a little country hotel doing the work that one could have done-instead of that, you would have one big organization controlling it all, thereby cutting out all this unnecessary duplication. That, to my mind, is a sound principle and that is really what the farmer is asking for to-day.
In the papers in eastern Canada-because I realize this is not so much a problem in eastern Canada as it is in the west-there is 312
a continual propaganda being carried on to make it appear that the federal government is simply bonusing bankrupt and down-and-out farmers of western Canada, and complaining of the injustice that is done to people in this section of the country in having to lend money to these men, who, they say, have squandered their holdings in riotous living. These articles in the papers in eastern Canada put the farmers of western Canada in a most humiliating position, a position they do not want to be in. I am quite sure that if the government built up the system that Doctor Tory suggests, the farmer will have to come here only when he has good security to offer, and he will secure his money at a very much reduced rate of interest and have payments spread over a long period of years. I do not know why some such system should not have been adopted. I appreciate the fact that it will take a considerable length of time to build up this land bank system, and probably the Acting Minister of Finance has decided in his wisdom that his present plan is merely an emergency measure, and that later on the question will be dealt with in this more constructive way. But I want to point out to him that we are losing valuable time. Doctor Tory points out that it is impossible for western agriculture to get on its feet and become re-established until some such system as this is evolved, and I think we all realize that. We spend days and days in this House discussing the tariff and a good many other things that, after all, are secondary to this question of rural credits in so far as western Canada is concerned. It is not much use to hold out a reduction of the tariff to a farmer whose debts are all due, and whose interest rates are eight and ten per cent, and who knows that possibly next year or the year after he will be forced off his farm, that the mortgage company or the bank is waiting for some immigrant with a few hundred dollars to come in to whom they can resell his farm. The only thing that can appeal to that man is some system under which his debts can be spread over a long period of years and his interest rate be greatly reduced.
It is pointed out by Doctor Tory that the difference between the current rate of interest and the rate that is secured by the farmers under the land bank system in the United States-we will say 5i or 6 per cent-would in the course of thirty or thirty-five years pay off the whole principal; that is, if the farmer in western Canada who is paying 8 per cent on a loan to-day had that interest reduced to 6 per cent, and he still continued



Rural Credits
paying the same amount that he is paying to-day, that difference of 2 per cent applied annually on principal would in that period pay off the entire loan. That is the principle on which the land bank system is based. I hope that in dealing with the question, the government has not acceded too readily to the demands of the mortgage companies because, after all, these mortgage companies are not going to go out of business. If they have funds to invest, and most of them have funds that are handed* to them by insurance companies and trust funds of various kinds, these funds can still be invested in the bonds of the land bank system, and they will not have to have this expensive field service which they are now maintaining. I believe in the end they will be just as well off. The insurance companies and the trust companies would have their money invested in a much sounder and safer way than they are to-day. The farmers would be welded together in one great organization where they would have to stand or fall together. The farmer who. perhaps, was a little more farseeing, had a little better business judgment than his less fortunate neighbour would be obliged to keep supervision over that neighbour because under this plan he has some interest in his neighbour's loan. That is a sound principle, and I would heartily recommend to the minister that he consider this at some future time and try to build up a system on the basis of the American land bank plan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend's point is covered by a previous clause which has been enacted and which enables the appointment of returning officers considerably before any election. The idea there was to meet the kind of problem my hon. friend has in mind, letting the returning officer get his ballot boxes and have everything on hand.

No. I
would like to explain to the Prime Minister how this works. Take for instance the last election in West Edmonton. The ballots have to be printed after nomination day, and we have a two-days-a-week service from Edmonton north over the railway running into northern Alberta, either to Waterways or Peace river. Going one hundred miles down the Peace river, by sleigh or otherwise, there is a period in the fall when the river is not open and the boats are unable to navigate, yet the ice will not bear a team. During that period it is very difficult to make the trip in ten days or even two weeks. In the spring when the ice is breaking there is the same trouble. That is the reason, I understand, that at the last election three or four 312i
polls down the Peace river did not secure ballots, although they had two weeks' time.

My hon.
friend will realize that in the last election the returning officer did not know he was going to be appointed to that position until a short time before polling.
Oh, yes.

What difference does that,
make in regard to the ballots?
A great deal of difference, for the simple reason that if you have a permanent returning officer, such as described by the act. he will have to pick out his deputy returning officers for each poll.
You do not keep the ballots on hand?

No, we do
not keep them on hand. My hon. friend is getting too gay.
Is it not a fact that the ballots will have to be printed after nomination day?
Yes.
And it is suggested that there will be a difficulty in getting the ballots to the polling place.
I quite apprehend that. My hon. friend said ten days might be occupied in doing that work.
No.

The point
that must be kept in view in regard to that is this: Suppose all returning officers in Canada were appointed next month, they would have iall the preliminary work done and arrangements made. In addition to that, under former conditions, no returning officer could be picked out beforehand. Under the new act all that can be arranged and all preliminary matters provided in such a way that only under the most exceptional circumstances would it be possible that the ballots could not reach the polling place in time. It does not seem wise to butcher up the act by making exceptions for conditions which only arise under the most unusual circumstances.

I should
like to point out that in this case the returning officer in the last election, Mr. Hunt, of Edmonton, knew his business, and it was not through any neglect or lack of knowledge or anything of that sort, 'but arose owing to the difficult conditions of travel from the city of

Edmonton to the Peace river and Fort Vermilion down the Peace river. We have a large settlement there, large enough to have an experimental farm, and they have a right to be protected so far as it can be done. In a constituency where to certain points the distance to be travelled is 650 miles from the point where the returning officer is located, it is not unreasonable to ask for three weeks' time, especially where the ballot 'boxes must be delivered by team.

Would the fact that the
returning officers are to be appointed beforehand make any difference?
None whatever, because in this case the returning officer knew his 'business.
What is t'he objection to the six weeks period we have had in the past?

We have not had it in the
past, except in the last election, where it was provided that two weeks should expire between nomination and polling. Representations have come from a great many constituencies that that period is too long. Before the election of 1921 we had only seven days between nomination and polling and that provision was changed in 1921. In the great majority of constituencies throughout Canada it was recommended that seven days was a long enough period, but some of the larger constituencies such as those mentioned by my hon. friend are exceptions, and to take care of those constituencies the period is left at two weeks; in all other constituencies it is seven days, and that seems to be the consensus of opinion.

The minister said that
certain representations have been made for a change. What are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was thought advisable, I understand, to have all the elections on the same day. That is why the period of fifteen days was put in the statute instead of seven days, which has always been the period since confederation. Why should 220 constituencies of Canada suffer by reason of the fact that in fourteen or fifteen constituencies seven days is not sufficient delay? It has been thought advisable to have the same system as prevailed in some other provinces. In the province of Quebec, in the large constituencies, nomination takes place seven days before nominations are made in the other ridings; so that the same end will be obtained and elections will be held on the same day. In some fourteen or fifteen constituencies
(Mr. D. M. KenneUy.l
nomination will take place seven days earlier. Surely fifteen days is sufficient time between nomination and polling, and I cannot believe that my hon. friend is serious in asking that three weeks should elapse between nomination and polling day. He does not want to be electioneering all the year.

I am
serious, all right.

My hon. friend says 220
constituencies would suffer. In what way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because df the increased expense and trouble. Everybody knows that the real election starts on nomination day in most constituencies. Perhaps this is not the case in my hon. friend's constituency, but the big work is done between nomination and polling. We have to hold our committees in all the different places, and it is expensive for poor men like myself.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

I desire to point out some objections I offered in the special committee to which this bill was referred. I think it is desirable that the day of nomination throughout the Dominion should be uniform, as is the day of election. The Elections Act as it stood before provided for fourteen days between the day of nomination and the day of polling, but the act as reported by the committee reduced it to seven, except as regards certain large constituencies named in the schedule. I contend that fourteen days is short, enough in any case. Let us see what the returning officer has to do. He cannot assume until after the nomination that there will be a contest. It is true, as pointed out by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou), that he can make a certain amount of preliminary preparation, but there is much to be done and much that cannot be done until after nomination. He must get. his ballots printed. Suppose there is no printing office where the returning officer lives-and this is not at. all improbable-he will then have fo get in touch with one probably some distance from his residence. As we all know, printing offices at election times are crowded with work; they have more than they can do. There is therefore always a delay in the printing of ballots at these smaller offices. When the ballots are returned to him, after perhaps two or three days' delay in the printing office,

Elections Act
the returning officer must stamp every one of them with a special stamp. Then he has to sort them and get them in their proper quantities for distribution to his deputies. He must also distribute his ballot boxes to the deputies, and the instructions contained in the act require that the ballot boxes shall be distributed by -mail wherever this is possible. Then he has to swear in his deputies and make all preliminary arrangements for the poll. If there is bad weather and the roads are in poor shape there may be delays in the mailing of the boxes, which must reach the deputy returning officer in time. This is unfair to the deputy returning officer, because if we allow only seven days between nomination and polling it will leave practically no time for him to become familiar with all his duties. And the act is not at all easy to understand, nor is it easy to comply with all its requirements. Formerly when the seven-day period was allowed, we all know, it often happened that the deputy did not get the ballot boxes until midnight of the day before polling, and he went into the polling booth poorly equipped for his duties. That will happen again. I fear therefore that we shall have very serious errors some of which probably will invalidate elections. There is not enough time if you reduce the period from fourteen to seven days.

As to the instructions to the
returning officer, they are given as soon as the writs are issued.

He will have,
no doubt, a certain circular containing instructions, but he will not have all the material necessary to equip himself properly for the discharge of his duties. There are certain other provisions of the act with reference to nomination day which I submit cannot be complied with in seven days. The statute provides that at least two days before polling the boxes shall be delivered to each returning officer. That cannot be done if we allow only seven days between nomination and polling; the returning officer will not have sufficient time to have the ballots printed, stamped and distributed in four days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

But this act is
much more complicated; there is much more to be done by the returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not so far as the

He has to stamp all the ballots, and that is a comparatively new provision; it was not done many years ago. Schedule (a) of rule 15, at page 128 of the pamphlet copy of the act provides that on the twelfth day before polling day the revising officer shall perform certain duties, but he cannot perform those duties if nomination day is only seven days before polling.

Those would apply to
the old act.

No, they still
remain in the act.

days stands, there must be a change, but the act does not refer to that.
What section is my hon. friend referring to?

To rule 15 of
schedule A. It says that:
On the twelfth day before the polling day the revising officer shall,-
(b) deliver or mail by registered letter to each of the candidates a statement of such changes,-
And so on. The printing of these voters' lists is not to be done until after nomination day. How is that possible if the seven-day period stands? This whole act is framed on the'basis that fourteen days shall elapse between nomination and polling, and the duties are to be discharged on that basis. Rule 5 at page 135 provides that:
Every registrar having revised and corrected such retained copy of the voters' list compiled by him shall write at the foot of such copy and close to the last name thereon, on the ninth day before the polling day, a certificate in the form of (the certificate contained in said form No. 11 to this act. How can he do that if the nomination is not until seven days before the election? I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it should be at least fourteen days as in the old act.

Mr. Chairman, I had
something to do with this act when it was originally prepared and passed through the House, and at that time, after careful calcula-

tion, it was considered that fourteen days was the least time that could elapse between nomination day and polling day. The idea in the first instance was not to change the old seven-day limit, but it was found that the act could not be worked out in seven days, and consequently fourteen days was inserted. The	CHAIRMAN: He suggested an

This is a rather difficult clause, and I am very much confused in regard to it because it affects almost entirely the province of Ontario. The act as passed in 1920 provides that in every province the provincial lists, where there are provincial lists, are to be taken as the basis for the preparation of the voters' lists. The registrar is instructed to take that provincial list and from it to make up his preliminary list for further revision. During the last election the Chief Electoral Officer had some difficulty in regard to Ontario. The Secretary of State is
quite right in saying that when the act was passed in 1920, the intention was to utilize the provincial lists, where provincial lists were in existence, as the bas:s for the preparation of the Dominion list, and the clause was inserted in the act providing that where provincial lists existed that were not more than two years old, they should be accepted as the basis for the Dominion list. In the amendment as prepared to-day by the Chief Electoral Officer, the two-year clause is omitted, and it leaves Ontario in this position. ,Under the provincial law the voters' lists are prepared in three parts, parts I and II apply to municipal voters and provincial voters. Part III of the Ontario list applies only to provincial voters or manhood franchise voters. Part III is a list which is never actually completed unless a provincial election is pending. It is the duty of the municipal clerk annually to prepare such a list as part III, but until word is received from the Provincial Secretary, the list is not printed. It

But it was printed for the purpose of taking the vote on the Ontario Temperance Act. I believe it was looked upon as a very complete and excellent list. The vote upon that list took place on the 23rd October of last year and it is still available, I believe. But the trouble is this. Municipal clerks, in many instances in Ontario, have treated that as an ejection list although it was only for the purpose of a plebiscite, and they have not this year made up part- III at all. In some municipalities part III exists, but in others it is said that part III has not been prepared and will not be printed or available until probably December 1 of the present year. It is rumoured that we might posibly have an election this year, and if that election comes before 1st December, I doubt if there would be in existence provincial lists containing part III which is the large body of manhood franchise voters. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the following information, I think, should be sufficient to convince the committee of the undesirability of this amendment. The other day I asked the Chief Electoral Officer to find

Elections Act
out what time had elapsed between the date of the issuing of the writs and the date of the poll in every general election since confederation. The first three elections having taken place on different days, it was not possible to give the figures, but he has supplied me with the following information:	In the
election of 1878 the writ was issued on August 17 and the date of the poll was September 17 -31 days. For the other elections the respective dates were: 1882, May 18 and June 20-33 days; 1887, January 17 and February 22-36 days; 1891, February 4 and March 5- 29 days; 1896,-hon. members will recall that the Tupper administration had stayed in office the full five years, and they stretched the interval to the full sixty days; this is the only occasion where sixty days have elapsed between the issuing of the writ and the date of the election, the respective dates being April 24 and June 23; 1900, October 9 and November 7-29 days; 1904, September 29 and November 3-35 days; 1908, August 3 and September 21 -49 days; 1917, October 31 and December 17 -47 days; 1921-the last election-October 8 and December 6-59 days. Now, my hon. friend from Humboldt suggests that we should make the period sixty days. Well, I ask the committee if that would not be an intolerable situation? It does not follow, as has been said repeatedly, that because the writs must issue on a certain date the elections will necessarily be limited within that period. The last election began in the month of August and ended on December 6. According to the statement of the Chief Electoral Officer forty-five days is the least possible time within which the polling could take place after the issuing of the writs, assuming that everything goes without a hitch. The government in planning the date of the election unquestionably will be governed by the advice of the Chief Electoral Officer, and with forty-five days as the minimum, and nothing to restrict us in the other direction- to take as many extra days as we want, I submit it would be very foolish for the House to bind itself to a period of sixty days.
May I again remind the House that there is a certain obligation on our part to the business community not to have the country in a state of turmoil over an unnecessarily lengthy period, and while sixty days might serve a useful purpose on one occasion, on other occasions it would be altogether too long a time. Having regard to the circumstance that in all the previous elections, with the exception of the one that I have referred to, sixty days has been found unnecessary and has never been used, I submit that there is
no necessity at this stage of our development to alter our election law in that regard. May I point out this further circumstance, that in the early elections the constituencies were much larger than they are to-day, that they were more sparsely settled, and that the means of transportation did not begin to be what they are to-day; we had fewer railways and the automobile was unknown. Why should we at this time want to take up a period for election purposes that all our governments since confederation have found wholly unnecessary and inadvisable?

Mr. Chairman,
I desire to point out two or three respects in which our election machinery has changed over the period referred to by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let us change the machinery and not the period.

There is good
reason for lengthening the period because the machinery has changed. The right hon. gentleman will recall that in the earlier years we had a Dominion franchise that differed from the provincial franchise; and we had our own lists which were prepared and ready in advance of an election. I think it would be about 1900, or some time shortly after, that the Dominion franchise was repealed and we adopted the franchises of the various provinces, and also their lists. The last act provided for bringing the lists down to date by registration in towns and by enumerators in rural districts, and a great deal of machinery was set up, involving a lot of work in connection with elections to-day under this act that formerly had not been necessary. All this work has to be done from the issue of the writ, everything dates from that time, and really sixty days is not too long an interval within which to accomplish it. Any shorter period does not give the candidate an opportunity to take all the steps in connection with his campaign to which he is entitled and which are necessary. I think sixty days is not at all too long between the issue of the writ and the polling.
